comments.body:
## Phase 1 RCA — mechanism proven; classified `incomplete-implementation` (cited); ESCALATED on AC3 design decision

Investigated under /rebar-debug in a fresh worktree off `origin/main`
(`565e1856bc9d180876fdbcaa336ccd57ceb8202e`; the 2337 fix `83edf99` is an ancestor).
Step 0: no duplicate ticket; sole report. Reported-against floor = current `origin/main`.

### Proven mechanism (the guards are genuinely ABSENT — an omission, not broken behaviour)

- **AC1/AC2 (mint-time warning) — absent.** `sign_manifest` → `_sign_manifest_under_lock` →
  `_prepare_manifest_event` → `mint_opcert_record` (`src/rebar/_opcert_signing.py:293`) resolves
  the signing key via `ensure_opcert_key`/`_opcert_own_key_paths` and mints, but never invokes the
  verify-side resolver `_opcert_own_public_keys` to check whether a public counterpart is
  resolvable. Confirmed statically: `_opcert_own_public_keys` has exactly ONE caller —
  `verify_opcert_record` (`_opcert_signing.py:550`) — and none on the mint path. So no warning is
  emitted when the public half is unresolvable.
- **AC3 (startup/deploy health check) — absent.** No public-counterpart / `_opcert_own_*` /
  `_read_opcert_pub` check exists anywhere in `mcp_server.py`, `_mcp_health.py`, or
  `_opcert_binding.py` (grep: zero hits). `compose_startup_opcert_binding` (`mcp_server.py:717`)
  validates only the PRIVATE key (present / 0600 / Ed25519 / not-encrypted, via `compose_signer`)
  and aborts startup on an unusable signer — it never checks that a public counterpart is
  resolvable.

These are `static` (content) hypotheses, confirmed by source + reference-set inspection; there is
no runtime failure to reproduce because the whole defect is a SILENCE.

### Legitimacy: `incomplete-implementation` (cited), NOT a fresh feature request

Design authority establishing these guards were *meant to exist*:
- Parent bug `d26a-8ffa-97cd-4b2a` (`dire-expectable-terrapin`), closed `plan_defect`, explicitly
  scoped **AC5 (mint-time WARNING) + AC6 (deploy/startup health check)** and SPLIT them into this
  ticket as "additive guards against the class regressing." That parent plan passed plan-review.
- Designed-but-unwired seams already in-repo: the verify-side `_opcert_own_public_keys` resolver
  (AC1), the `run_startup_store_sweep` startup-warning idiom (AC1), and the fail-closed startup
  validator `compose_startup_opcert_binding` (AC3).

So approval is NOT the open question → not a `feature-request`, not `intended-behavior`. This is a
deferred, scoped omission = `incomplete-implementation`.

**Attribution (scope-of-work).** This is an omission, so there is no introducing commit that
"broke" it. By scope-of-work it attributes to `d26a-8ffa-97cd-4b2a` — the ticket whose acceptance
criteria (AC5/AC6) the missing behaviour falls under, which shipped the key-resolution fix without
these deferred guards.

### Why I am ESCALATING rather than auto-fixing (per operator instruction)

The mint-time warning (AC1/AC2) is cleanly auto-fixable: purely additive, non-refusing, fully
pinned by the cited authority (warn, naming the resolved key path + principal; do not refuse; the
existing success path and returned signature are unchanged). Mirrors `run_startup_store_sweep`.

**AC3 is NOT pinned by the cited authority** — it "requires a design decision" and "alters
deploy-time behaviour," which the operator reserved for themselves. AC3 says the health check
"FAILS," but the repo contains TWO deliberate, conflicting precedents:

- **(a) Hard-abort startup** — extend the existing fail-closed `compose_startup_opcert_binding`
  (which already aborts on an unusable signer). Scoped to the on-box signing deploy only (both
  `REBAR_OPCERT_ENV_ID` + `REBAR_IDENTITY_SIGNING_KEY` set); dev/stdio/genesis returns `None`
  early and is unaffected; a correctly-configured deploy (post-2337, which derives the public line
  in-process) still passes. Only a misconfigured signing deploy newly refuses to serve.
- **(b) Report a degraded field, never abort** — mirror `store_status` / `/health` +
  blue-green readiness gate. `_mcp_health.py` documents the explicit invariant: "a health probe
  that can fail is worse than one that reports a degraded field," and `run_startup_store_sweep` is
  log-and-continue ("a missing store must not abort boot"; only `RemovedInputError` fails hard).

These behave materially differently on a misconfigured deploy (refuse-to-serve vs serve-degraded),
and the choice is not resolved by the cited authority. Per the operating instruction to escalate
design decisions / behaviour changes, I am handing this call to the operator.

**Recommendation:** proceed on AC1/AC2 as specified; for AC3 adopt **option (a)** (extend
`compose_startup_opcert_binding`, gated on the on-box signing deploy) — it is the closest existing
precedent ("an unusable signer aborts startup"), fail-closed matches the parent bug's whole point
(silently-uncertifiable attestations are worse than a refused boot), and it has zero blast radius
on dev/stdio and on correctly-configured deploys. If the operator prefers non-aborting deploy
posture, option (b) is the alternative. Awaiting direction before Phase 2 / any Gerrit push.
No `--force` or gate bypass was used; no code change pushed.

compiled_state.description:
## Context / Problem
Split out of `d26a-8ffa-97cd-4b2a` (`dire-expectable-terrapin`), where these were carried as
its DEFERRED AC5 and AC6. That bug fixed the key-path DIVERGENCE that made the deployed MCP
server sign op-certs it could never verify (Gerrit 2337, merged as
`83edf9972728ae1e0729a39098ec70e4fab4617a`): verification now resolves the public half from the
same ordered chain the signing side resolves the private half.

What that fix did NOT add is any GUARD. `sign_manifest` still mints a certificate without
checking that the environment can resolve a public counterpart for the key it just signed
under, and nothing at deploy/startup fails when it cannot. So the CLASS of defect — a
silently uncertifiable attestation — can regress the moment a new deployment shape puts the
signing key somewhere the resolution chain does not reach. Signing succeeds; only a later
`verify_signature` (or a refused claim) reveals the problem, potentially long after the
certificates were minted.

## Approach
Two independent, additive guards, neither of which changes an existing success path:

1. At MINT: after resolving the signing key, ask the verify-side resolver
   (`_opcert_own_public_keys`, `src/rebar/_opcert_signing.py`) whether a public counterpart is
   resolvable for it. If not, emit an explicit WARNING naming the resolved key path and the
   principal. It must NOT refuse — refusing would break every existing sign flow and is a
   behaviour change beyond this bug's scope.
2. At STARTUP/DEPLOY: the MCP server's existing health surface (`src/rebar/_mcp_health.py`)
   fails when the bound signing key has no usable public counterpart, so the condition is
   caught before any certificate is minted rather than after.

Both are in-process checks driven by an operation and by server startup, with no dependency on
any particular CI provider.

## Scope
- In scope: the mint-time warning and the startup health check.
- Out of scope: the key-resolution chain itself (already fixed by 2337); any change to the
  cross-environment `foreign_key` verdict, which is documented intended behaviour (ADR 0104),
  not a defect.

## Testing
Unit tests: a mint under a key whose public half cannot be resolved emits the warning and still
returns a signature; a mint under a resolvable key emits no warning; the startup check fails for
the unresolvable key and passes for the resolvable one.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: `sign_manifest` emits an explicit WARNING — naming the resolved key path and the principal — when the environment cannot resolve a public counterpart for the key it just signed under, and still returns the signature (no refusal, no existing sign flow broken).
- [ ] AC2: `sign_manifest` emits no such warning when the public counterpart IS resolvable.
- [ ] AC3: the MCP server's startup/deploy health check fails when the signing key has no usable public counterpart, and passes when it has one.
- [ ] AC4: both guards are in-process and operation-linked, with no dependency on a specific CI provider.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] DD1: AC1 and AC2 covered by a test that is RED before the change and GREEN after it.
- [ ] DD2: AC3 covered by a test over the startup health check.
compiled_state.title: No guard surfaces a signing key with no usable public counterpart: sign_manifest stays silent and startup does not fail
